newsitem.title: INDIA: Bangladesh PM hopeful of water pact with India.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM hopeful of water pact with India.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said on Wednesday she hoped to reach an agreement with India on the sharing of Ganges River water, a deal that is seen as crucial to her political future.
Hasina told reporters after a ceremonial reception at the Presidential Palace in New Delhi that she could give no details until the end of the talks.
"Discussions are going on. So I think after everything is settled, then we can say," she said.
Asked if she expected to finalise agreements with India by the end of her three-day visit on Thursday, she said: "I am hopeful."
The sharing of disputed Ganges water, crucial to the economies of both India and Bangladesh, is considered a major political test for Hasina.
The Ganges river flows through northern India before emptying into the Bay of Bengal in Bangladesh.
Dhaka says India holds back water during the annual January-June dry season and releases excessive quantities during monsoon rains, causing flooding.
An agreement in 1977 to guarantee a minimum amount of water released from India was dropped five years later.
Hasina's Awami League party regained power in elections this year, 21 years after her father, independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, was assassinated in a bloody military coup.
Rahman became Bangladesh's first president after the Indian army helped him by fighting a war with Pakistan, which led to the breaking away of East Pakistan to become Bangladesh in 1971.

Hasina met Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral in the Presidential Palace after being received by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, who was scheduled to host a dinner for the visiting leader on Wednesday.
She later met former Foreign Minister Pranab Mukherjee and Sitaram Kesri, president of India's Congress party.

While water-sharing topped her agenda, Hasina was also expected to discuss the future of a 25-year-old friendship treaty that her father signed in March 1972. The accord has been criticised as a compromise to India by Hasina's rivals.
Asked if she expected a new long-term agreement with India, Hasina said: "I think after everything is finalised, then you will see."

But her party said before elections this year that there was no need to renew the 1972 accord because the formation of the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), including both nations, served the same purpose.

Hasina was also scheduled to meet President Shankar Dayal Sharma and Vice-President K.R. Narayanan, leader of the opposition Atal Behari Vajpayee of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and parliament speaker Purno Sangma, during her visit.

Later on Wednesday, she was expected to call on Sonia Gandhi, the Italian-born widow of former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, who wields considerable influence in Indian public affairs although she does not hold any office of significance.
Hasina was accompanied by Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad and Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak.
Delegations from the two countries were to meet at 7 p.m. (1330 GMT). They were expected to sign a water-sharing agreement on Thursday before Hasina leaves India.
Hasina arrived in India on Tuesday and spent her first day in the western state of Rajasthan, where she offered prayers at a revered Moslem saint's tomb in Ajmer city.
